text:
Anthropic has launched Claude Frontier Academy, a $100 million initiative built around a 12-week residency that trains AI engineers the way hospitals train doctors. The company aims to certify 10,000 Frontier Deployed Engineers (FDEs) by the end of 2027, with the first cohorts already underway at firms including Accenture, Bain, Capgemini, Deloitte, McKinsey, Morgan Stanley, Novo Nordisk, and Commonwealth Bank of Australia.

Why Anthropic is betting on training over hiring

According to the report, Anthropic sees engineers capable of taking AI from concept to a working enterprise system as the hardest talent to find in the current market, prompting the company to build that expertise itself rather than wait for it to emerge organically.

A medical-residency model, not a course

The programme deliberately mirrors how doctors are trained: learning from practitioners, working on real cases, and being formally assessed before working independently. It opens with a multi-day, in-person session led by Anthropic engineers and licensed instructors, covering a simulated enterprise deployment from use-case selection through security review. Clearing a graded practical exam at this stage earns participants the Claude Resident Engineer badge. The 12-week residency that follows has each engineer lead an actual Claude deployment at their own organisation, supported by Anthropic engineers, before a final assessment determines who earns the Claude Frontier Deployed Engineer badge, with the first badges expected in early 2027.

Selective access, not open enrolment

Seats are nomination-only. Companies put forward their strongest hands-on engineers, each arriving with a named Claude project to lead, and Anthropic is prioritising a track record of building with large language models over prior AI-agent experience specifically. Cohorts are currently running in San Francisco, New York, and London. "Claude Frontier Academy trains people the way our own engineers learn," said Steve Corfield, Anthropic's global head of business development and partnerships, per the report.

Part of a broader industry shift toward 'Forward Deployed' roles

The FDE title borrows from the forward-deployed engineer model Palantir popularised by embedding engineers directly inside client organisations. Data cited in the report from Draup shows FDE job openings across five major consulting firms climbed to 1,404 in the year ending May, even as overall postings at those firms fell roughly 24 percent. The Academy builds on Anthropic's existing Claude Partner Network, where professionals at 46,000 firms already hold more than 175,000 Claude certifications, with the company describing its 10,000-engineer target as just the first step.

text:
Reuters – L’Oreal OREP.PA has engaged restructuring advisers to explore options for rising US legal liabilities linked to its use of talc and other chemical ingredients in some of its cosmetic products, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday.

The cosmetics maker’s US unit is working with restructuring counsel Weil Gotshal & Manges and investment bank Ducera Partners to address lawsuits from individuals alleging the talc products caused illness, the Journal said, citing people familiar with the matter.

L’Oreal said in its latest half-year report that about 760 US proceedings over the alleged presence of asbestos particles in some talc-containing cosmetic products were pending as of June 30, up from about 620 at the end of 2025, and that it strongly contests the claims.

The Journal said L’Oreal is considering moving tort liabilities into a separate corporate entity to unload them through a sale to an outside investor, allowing the company to separate its exposure from its operating businesses.

As an option to address the claims outside Chapter 11, L’Oreal’s advisers are exploring a sale similar to Honeywell’s HON.Odivestiture last year of certain asbestos liabilities to corporate liability acquisition platform Delticus, the Journal said.

L’Oreal, Weil Gotshal & Manges and Ducera did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.

More broadly, talc litigation has cost Johnson & Johnson JNJ.N billions of dollars in a legal fight lasting more than a decade, and has prompted several companies to try to resolve claims in bankruptcy court.

In July, J&J said it would pay an estimated $5.5 billion to resolve tens of thousands of lawsuits alleging its baby powder and other talc products cause ovarian cancer. It had earlier filed for three bankruptcies through a shell-company subsidiary in an effort to settle the cases, though each ended in dismissal.

Avon Products, a US-based holding company of the Avon beauty brand, started Chapter 11 proceedings in 2024 to address its debt and talc liabilities.

L’Oreal is also facing thousands of lawsuits alleging its hair relaxer products could cause cancer in women. Arizona sued L’Oreal and its US subsidiary in September, alleging the cosmetics company hid evidence that the products could cause cancer.

text:
OpenAI has admitted its actions were "not good enough" after one of its rogue agents breached Australian government websites in June, saying it had added more precautions to its training environments.

The company's chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI on Tuesday in Sydney, saying the breach "should not have happened" and it "should have handled our response better". It took weeks before Australia was notified via an email to a generic inbox.

"We are sorry and we know we have work to do to rebuild trust with the Australian people," Kwon said.

Anthropic also appeared and said it had not found any cases of Australian breaches during a recent investigation.

Executives from Microsoft and Google were also present.

An OpenAI agent went "rogue" and "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare in June, in what cyber-security experts said was the first hack of its kind.

When asked why OpenAI had not directly contacted government ministers immediately after it found out about the breaches, Kwon acknowledged it was a mistake.

"In retrospect, we should have done what you're suggesting," Kwon said.

"The reason why it happened the way that it did is I think people were thinking about this as a technical situation and they wanted to contact the technical counterparties, but it's not good enough."

Kwon said the company has changed how it handles such incidents.

"Even if we don't fully understand the situation, we are just going to notify and start working through the situation collaboratively with the impacted party."

OpenAI has also added "more precautions" to its training environments since the incidents, Kwon told the 12-member committee, which is made up of Labor, Liberal and independent MPs and senators looking at AI and its impact on Australia.

The company was also establishing a local taskforce in Australia to investigate "how to better manage the risks associated with increasingly capable AI", it said.

Kwon told the committee that training models were now monitored in real time during tests, and that an alarm was triggered if they interacted with the internet in a way they were not meant to.

This meant that OpenAI had been able to alert the New South Wales government to another hack last week within 48 hours.

The company would also support a framework on mandatory disclosure of incidents, Kwon said, as it would set out "clear expectations".

"We were trying to come up with a standard to apply to our voluntary actions… Based on our learned experience here, we should have been probably talking to more people about how to do that well."

Anthropic's head of safeguards Dave Orr said that in the wake of OpenAI agents hacking tech platform Hugging Face in July, it had reviewed "hundreds of millions of transcripts" to detect any potential breaches of Australian government websites similar to OpenAI.

"We haven't found anything like this and we have looked," he told the committee.

The public hearings, which will continue until Friday, also heard evidence from arts and media organisations about copyright and their concerns on how AI models use their materials. AI companies want Australia to relax copyright laws so they can use books and music, for example, to train their AI models.

An opt-out model - where the onus would be on the artist to ask AI not to use their material for training purposes - was flawed and could mean artists do not get paid for their content, the committee heard.

"In other words, Australia's artists will be the roadkill in the rush to this AI deal," said Annabelle Herd, chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association.

Anthropic's special envoy Jeff Bleich told the hearing the company had "never tried to dictate" to Australia on its copyright laws.

text:
Nvidia Corp.'s $20 billion deal with Groq Inc. is facing a legal challenge from investors who say Groq’s senior leaders were driven by lucrative side agreements to help the AI giant eliminate an existential threat.

Two former Groq shareholders are targeting the transaction in Delaware’s Chancery Court, where their lawsuit against Groq’s former board and CEO was unsealed Monday. The unusual “reverse acqui-hire,” which involved buying most of Groq’s assets and hiring most of its staff, offered a financial windfall to the corporate directors who signed off on it, according to the legal filing.

For Nvidia, which isn’t named as a defendant, the business logic was allegedly straightforward: heading off inroads by a startup flush with positive press about its prospect of exploiting its breakthrough “word-by-word” processing capabilities to capture the AI throne. But across the table, the arrangement involved “flagrant breaches of fiduciary duty” that “cost Groq’s stockholders billions of dollars,” according to the proposed class action.

The board “handed Nvidia Groq’s valuable technology and the engineers who built Groq, took billions of dollars in benefits for itself, senior management, and affiliated funds that it did not share with Groq’s other stockholders, and then squeezed out those stockholders at a lowball price it set itself,” the suit says.

Groq’s former leaders are set to be represented by Alex Spiro, a a high-profile partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan LLP whose roster of celebrity clients has included Elon Musk, former New York Mayor Eric Adams, Jay-Z, and Alec Baldwin. A company spokesperson said in a statement Monday that the transaction “delivered exceptional value for Groq, our investors, and our employees.”

“This lawsuit is meritless and we will vigorously defend ourselves against it,” the spokesperson said. “We remain focused on serving our customers and building the world’s leading AI inference cloud.”

‘New Structures’

The deal last December, which has drawn antitrust and congressional scrutiny, is one of several recent corporate acquisitions aimed at growing and shoring up Nvidia’s dominant global position in the exploding trillion-dollar market for AI chips and related technology. The transactions also include its $13 billion deal for AI startup Hugging Face, which was announced last month.

The lawsuit zeroes in on the transaction’s unusual mechanics, which the filing describes as an attempt to end-run the antitrust concerns that would normally greet any acquisition by an overwhelming market leader, along with traditional M&A dynamics like shareholder approval. After giving Nvidia a steal on Groq’s tech and human resources, the board then cashed out public investors from the remaining “shell” company for an underpriced $3.5 billion, according to the filing.

“New structures must comply with the law, just like old ones,” the suit says. “Fortunately, drawing the line is easy in this case.”

The court complaint was originally filed under seal Sept. 29.

The Groq shareholders, Benjamin Serebrin and Joshua Robin, are represented by Bernstein Litowitz Berger & Grossmann LLP.

text:
Stablecoins, central bank digital currencies, and tokenized payment instruments could significantly reduce bank revenues if they do not start developing their own blockchain-based settlement solutions. According to Capgemini, up to $230 billion in banking revenue could be at risk.

Blockchain Payments Will Take a Share of the Global Market

These findings are contained in the Capgemini World Payments Report 2027. Analysts expect that by 2030, blockchain-based payment instruments will account for 4% of the total volume of payments worldwide.

For banks, this means pressure on several traditional sources of income at once: spreads on currency pairs, correspondent banking operations, commission fees, and other payment services. Currently, about $4 trillion in funds from large companies is held in bank accounts to support international transactions. As settlements using stablecoins, central bank digital currencies, and tokens become more widespread, this money could leave the banking system.

Large Businesses Are Ready to Switch to New Payment Systems

Capgemini surveyed representatives of 1,110 companies with annual revenues of more than $1 billion. About 60% of respondents said they are ready to abandon banking services in favor of blockchain payment systems if their banks cannot offer a comparable level of service.

At the same time, banks still have an opportunity to retain clients. If they provide convenient and cost-competitive settlements in stablecoins and cryptocurrencies, 71% of companies will continue to use banking services.

Banks Are Still Acting Cautiously

Among 300 surveyed representatives of the banking sector, only 21% reported that their organizations are actively developing blockchain-based payment instruments. In the near term, many bankers consider tokenization of bank deposits a more important area. They associate this approach with current legal practices and the desire to keep client funds within the banking system.

“At stake is $230 billion, so banks need to decide what role they want to play in this emerging ecosystem,” said Capgemini Head of Payments Jeroen Holscher.

Earlier, it was reported that Russian banks could lose annual revenues of 100 billion rubles due to the launch of the digital ruble.

name: Walmart
title: How Christina Zhu turned Sam's Club into Walmart's unlikely growth engine in China
description:
It entered China in 1996 with a Supercenter and a Sam’s Club in Shenzhen.
Walk into the Sam’s Club in Shenzhen’s Qianhai district, and the store feels disorientingly similar to one you might find in middle America.
“Sam’s Club is really the secret sauce to everything,” says Cameron Johnson, a senior partner at Tidal Wave Solutions.
“Sam’s Club is positioned very clearly: We serve upper-middle-class families in Chinese cities,” Zhu said.
Today, a door-to-door car charter to and from the Qianhai Sam’s Club costs 540 Hong Kong dollars ($69) on the travel platform Klook.
text:
As a child, she watched her parents wake up at 4:30 a.m. on Sundays to go to the wet market. “They had to haggle, and high-quality produce wasn’t always guaranteed,” Zhu, born in 1973, recalled at the Fortune Leaders Forum in Macau in September.

Today, Chinese shoppers are “probably the group with the most choices [in the world],” and they have become “the most demanding customers,” she said.

Meeting those rising expectations has become the defining challenge for retailers in China, and Walmart has managed it better than most. It entered China in 1996 with a Supercenter and a Sam’s Club in Shenzhen. Three decades later, the U.S. retailer is thriving in the world’s second-largest economy even as other foreign brands struggle.

China represents 3% of Walmart’s overall business, but it is growing, generating $24.6 billion in sales in its past fiscal year, a 19.3% jump. Sales grew 20.7% last quarter, faster than the 5.9% reported by the company as a whole.

Those figures are even more impressive given China’s ongoing consumption slump. Consumer-goods retail sales in China grew 1.1% in the first eight months of the year, compared with 4.6% growth over the same period in 2025, and just 0.4% year over year in August. High unemployment and a real-estate crisis are weighing on spending.

Walmart has defied the downturn by meeting the dual needs of the discerning Chinese consumer: extreme convenience, in the form of lightning-fast delivery, and an in-person shopping experience so novel that stores have become a holiday destination for shoppers throughout the region.

Walk into the Sam’s Club in Shenzhen’s Qianhai district, and the store feels disorientingly similar to one you might find in middle America. It has cavernous ceilings and shelves stacked with goods sold in generous bulk portions—only here it is gift boxes of mooncakes and abalone for the Mid-Autumn Festival instead of large tubs of mac and cheese or packs of beef franks.

The big-box membership warehouses are Walmart’s primary growth engine in China. Sam’s Clubs contribute about 70% of Walmart revenue in China, estimates Fitch Ratings senior director Cathy Chao, and the business has expanded from 15 clubs in 2016 to 67 in May.

“Sam’s Club is really the secret sauce to everything,” says Cameron Johnson, a senior partner at Tidal Wave Solutions. “People like the fact that it’s cheaper, and it still feels very premium and curated.”

Sam’s Club had 10.7 million members in China as of June, each paying at least 260 yuan ($39) per year for a basic membership. “Sam’s Club is positioned very clearly: We serve upper-middle-class families in Chinese cities,” Zhu said. “We think of ourselves less as a retailer, less as a channel … We are the buying agents for members.”

Staff at the Shenzhen Sam’s Club say that during holiday periods such as Chinese New Year, customers line up for more than an hour to get in. The clubs have even become a draw for tourists from Hong Kong, a city once synonymous with cross-border shopping in the other direction. Visitors hop across the Hong Kong-mainland border to fill their trolleys with roast chicken, toilet paper and bumper-size bottles of laundry detergent they cannot find at home.

In 2023, Hong Kong travel agencies began running package tours to Shenzhen’s Sam’s Club and competitor Costco: dinner and karaoke on day one, warehouse shopping on day two, and shipping back across the border arranged for anyone who bought too much to carry home. Today, a door-to-door car charter to and from the Qianhai Sam’s Club costs 540 Hong Kong dollars ($69) on the travel platform Klook.

Walmart hasn’t always been a hit in China. Since 2016, it has closed underperforming stores in favor of expanding Sam’s Club and its online offerings. Walmart is now generating more revenue than it did in 2019, when its China footprint was at its largest.

Much of Walmart’s China revival has happened under Zhu’s watch. In May 2020, the McKinsey and Honeywell alum joined Walmart as China president and CEO, becoming the first woman and first native Chinese person to hold the job.

Since then, her biggest priority has been making Walmart China digital-first. Its stores double as fulfillment centers, and Sam’s Club sits at the center of a “cloud warehouse” network that can deliver groceries to customers who do not live near a store.

“Convenience” for those living in other developed markets might mean receiving an order within three days. “Here, it’s 30 minutes,” Zhu said. Then-Walmart CEO Doug McMillon said last year that 80% of orders in China arrive within an hour. A Westerner might tolerate a 30-minute drive to a store, but a Chinese customer accepts only an eight-minute walk, Zhu said.

Foreign brands have struggled amid China’s economic slump and fierce domestic competition. Starbucks and Nike are losing ground to the likes of Luckin Coffee and Anta Sports.

Yet Walmart has “kept its foreign halo,” Johnson says, owing in part to high food-safety and quality-control standards and how well it has customized its offerings. “They’ve localized the marketing, the digitization, the supply chains, but they’ve kept their American-style service standards,” he says. Walmart China, for instance, has shrunk portion sizes to match households’ smaller appetites.

Even China’s notorious price wars—called neijuan, or “involution”—work in Walmart’s favor. They have forced the retailer to close or renovate weak stores and digitize operations to keep customers engaged.

When asked why Walmart has surged as other foreign brands stumble, Zhu put her own spin on founder Sam Walton’s most famous maxim: “I only have one boss, and my boss is the Chinese customer,” she said.

description:

Afin de régler ces réclamations en dehors du cadre du chapitre 11, les conseillers de L'Oréal étudient une cession similaire à celle réalisée l'année dernière par Honeywell

HON.O , qui avait cédé certaines responsabilités liées à l'amiante à la plateforme d'acquisition de passifs d'entreprise Delticus, a précisé le Journal.

Avon Products, une société holding basée aux États-Unis détenant la marque de beauté Avon, a entamé une procédure de redressement judiciaire au titre du chapitre 11 en 2024 afin de faire face à sa dette et à ses responsabilités liées au talc.

text:
Amazon hired former Microsoft Copilot CTO Pedram Rezaei to help the e-commerce and cloud giant build out its agentic AI business.

Rezaei joined AWS as a distinguished engineer in its Agentic AI and Emerging Technologies group, according to an email announcement on Monday.

He spent two decades at Microsoft, most recently training foundation models on the company's Superintelligence team. Rezaei served as Copilot's CTO until June and previously held senior technical roles in key product areas including search engine Bing and business software suite Dynamics 365.

At Amazon, Rezaei will initially work on Quick and Kiro, two products Amazon sees as central to its AI agent strategy, according to the email by Swami Sivasubramanian, the company's VP of agentic AI. An Amazon spokesperson shared the memo with Business Insider.

Quick is AWS's AI assistant and productivity app, while Kiro is an AI-powered coding tool. Quick's monthly AI users grew fourfold from the first to second quarter, while Kiro's user base doubled over the same period, Sivasubramanian noted in the email.

"Pedram joins at an exciting time for our organization as we continue to build out our technical leadership team to help take on the ambitious work we have planned," he wrote in the memo.

The hire gives Amazon an experienced builder from one of its biggest rivals at a moment when the company is trying to turn its AI investments into widely used products. Microsoft has made Copilot a centerpiece of its AI strategy. Amazon, meanwhile, has been building its own portfolio of AI tools, from its Bedrock model platform to coding assistants and agentic software.

Rezaei's arrival also suggests Amazon is making a stronger push in the AI agent space. The market is growing quickly, with new agent offerings such as OpenAI's Dots, Meta's Muse and Instinct gaining traction.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been shaking up leadership to accelerate its AI strategy. Two more high-profile executives are on the way out.

Peter Lee, a Microsoft veteran influential in the company's AI research, on Wednesday announced plans to leave.

The next day, Microsoft Office boss Ryan Roslansky said he'll be gone at the end of the year. Roslansky's departure was especially surprising as he was seen as a successor to longtime veteran Rajesh Jha, who retired in July. Roslansky was also a key part of Nadella's new inner circle and was one of three executives who made up Microsoft's new Copilot leadership team.

Here's the full email from Amazon's Sivasubramanian:

Team,

I'm happy to share that Pedram Rezaei is joining Agentic AI and Emerging Technologies as a Distinguished Engineer, effective today.

Pedram joins us after more than 20 years at Microsoft, most recently working on training foundation models and, before that, in senior architecture and CTO roles across Copilot, Power BI, and other products. He is a hands-on engineer who is still in the code every day, and he plans to keep it that way here. He lives in Seattle with his wife and their two young sons. Please join me in welcoming him.

As many of you know, we have a major opportunity with Quick and Kiro to transform how work gets done. The number of users for Kiro doubled from Q1 to Q2, while monthly AI users for Quick grew 4x. Initially, Pedram will help work to bolster these product areas. His plan for the first few months is straightforward: meet people, learn how things work here, and ship something real.

Pedram joins at an exciting time for our organization as we continue to build out our technical leadership team to help take on the ambitious work we have planned.

In addition, I want to take this opportunity to share some news with the wider team. As many of you know, we see our investments in Neurosymbolic AI and automated reasoning as one of our biggest bets for the future, and to help execute that vision, we've brought back Marvin Theimer and Reto Kramer. They've already been back for a little while now, and it's great to have them in the fold again.

Thanks for the warm welcome I know you'll extend to all three.

Swami

text:
As Convatec completes a multiyear effort to turn around the business, new CEO Jonny Mason plans to invest in research and development for future growth.

The London-based medtech firm, which specializes in infusion care, wound care, ostomy care and continence, announced plans last year to expand its Boston-based R&D facility by 50%, and open a new facility in Manchester, England.

Former CEO Karim Bitar joined Convatec in 2019 to develop a turnaround strategy for the company, which had struggled with profit warnings and a falling share price since it started trading on the London Stock Exchange. That plan involved focusing on Convatec’s strengths, doubling its R&D investment and upping capital spending to rebuild its factories. Unfortunately, Bitar died suddenly last October while on medical leave.

Mason, who joined Convatec in 2022 as CFO, has taken on Bitar’s legacy after being named CEO in October. The turnaround is complete, Mason said, and Convatec is now aiming for sales growth of 6% to 8% next year, supported by a series of new product launches in each of its categories.

MedTech Dive spoke with Mason about what’s next for the company and its investment plans.

Editor’s note: This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

MEDTECH DIVE: What are your top priorities as CEO? Is it a continuation of your work with Karim? Has anything changed?

JONNY MASON: Something has changed, which is that we’ve increased our ambition. Karim very successfully took us through the turnaround strategy, and we acknowledged that the turnaround was complete last year. So it was time to step up a level.

What Convatec is trying to do now is more than it’s ever done before. We are launching more products in 2026 than we’ve ever done before. We’re investing more capital. We’re increasing capacity in our factories. So all of that requires the whole Convatec organization to execute more effectively, and to live and breathe a culture of purpose and performance.

What segments do you see the most growth in for Convatec?

All four of our categories are going to grow faster next year than they did this year because we’re launching new products in all of those categories. But if you were to push me, infusion care is where our business is growing fastest, and that’s because pump therapy is expanding in its treatment of patients, both in diabetes and also in Parkinson’s disease. We’re the world leader in the manufacture of infusion sets. The use of pump therapy as opposed to pills or multiple daily injections is increasing quickly around the world. So that piece of our business, we expect that to grow in double digits from next year onwards.

What are some new devices to watch for?

In [the infusion care] space, the most exciting thing is Parkinson’s disease at the moment. AbbVie launched their Parkinson’s therapy a couple of years ago, and that’s growing really fast. And we are the exclusive supplier of infusion sets to them. But coming now are two other suppliers of Parkinson’s disease therapies: Supernus and Mitsubishi Tanabe. We will be launching with them the infusion sets to support their Parkinson’s therapy. Beyond that in infusion care, in a few years’ time, we’re working on higher volume and higher viscosity infusion sets, which will enable things like chemotherapy and/or pain relief to be treated with pump therapy.

We launched a new product only yesterday [September 28] in the U.S. market, and this was an intermittent catheter called Cure Aqua. It’s made of a hydrophilic polymer, which is friction free with just the application of water, and it’s ready to use and it’s in the value end of the market. So this is a product which is going to make life much better for a number of catheter users in the U.S.

We launched eight new products between 2022 and 2025. And then in 2026 and 2027, we’re doing eight more. So the pace of launch is accelerating.

At the start of the year, the FDA had raised concerns with infusion sets made by subsidiary Unomedical in a warning letter. Do you have any updates on that?

We are making good progress. We are in a very constructive dialog with the FDA. We understand exactly what their observations are. The observations did not relate to product quality nor to patient safety, and therefore they have not impacted our sales or our production at all. What they observed was that they said we weren’t managing our complaints process well enough, and we accept that entirely. We’re working with them to change it. They said the same thing, by the way, to various other operators within the diabetes sector.

We’re working constructively with them, making good progress. The nature of these things is that they take time, so we would like to think that we can get through all of this by the end of 2027.

Read More in Medical Devices

About a year ago, Convatec announced plans to invest $1 billion into R&D in the U.S. and the U.K. What else can you tell me about that?

description:
That’s why Wall Street is abuzz over Monday’s Microsoft note from closely watched analyst Ben Reitzes of Melius Research.
And even before that, he had been sounding the alarm that enterprise software stocks were vulnerable to AI disruption risks.
Microsoft has become less focused on the AI model layer and more on the harness layer.
Stephen Brashear | Getty Images News | Getty Images When a longtime holdout on a stock changes his tune, it’s a really big deal.
That’s why Wall Street is abuzz over Monday’s Microsoft note from closely watched analyst Ben Reitzes of Melius Research.
text:
When a longtime holdout on a stock changes his tune, it’s a really big deal. That’s why Wall Street is abuzz over Monday’s Microsoft note from closely watched analyst Ben Reitzes of Melius Research. Reitzes took the Club stock to a buy from hold, where his rating had been since a February downgrade. And even before that, he had been sounding the alarm that enterprise software stocks were vulnerable to AI disruption risks. Along with Monday’s upgrade, Reitzes also said that “at the risk of embarrassment,” he raised his price target all the way up to $665 from $465, implying more than 25% of upside to current levels around $525. Summed up in the title of his note, “The adults are in charge,” the analyst thinks that Microsoft’s experienced leadership and steady hand will be rewarded by clients and investors in this next leg of artificial intelligence. In Reitzes’ view, the recent freakout by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about AI safety, and follow-up from other key opinion leaders in the AI industry, served to strengthen the demand for Microsoft and the cyber companies needed to protect against the most severe concerns relating to data privacy and rogue AI agents. These more mature players will play “a key cog in the security, governance and the ‘AI CYA’ play that is likely in the early innings,” Reitzes wrote. Notably, Reitzes said he had felt this same way about Microsoft last year, before getting frustrated and more bearish due to issues with Azure and Copilot. Jim had also been frustrated with Microsoft. But as Jim always says, when the facts change, so should your opinion. His views did. And so have those of Reitzes, who said he is now ready to get more bullish on Microsoft, citing last month’s “repackaging of Copilot with Autopilot for agents may indeed be the product enterprises choose to corral potential chaos.” “Microsoft’s prospects in core apps and Azure are better than we previously thought, as it may be more insulated from agentic threats,” wrote Reitzes, who in 2024 predicted that AI will “eat a lot of software,” over the long term , a prescient call given the rise of the “SaaSpocalypse” narrative that took hold last year and reached a fever pitch earlier in 2026. We think Reitzes’ new argument is sound and aligns with Jim’s views that Microsoft’s Copilot pivot to enterprise makes it a safe space for companies to take advantage of AI for their businesses inside the protective embrace of the software platforms in which they are already heavily embedded. Put another way, fear of AI — be it an outside hack or the risk that an AI tool goes rogue — will solidify demand for those, like Microsoft, that can best protect against the risks. Enterprise customers appear more willing to bear the additional costs because it’s better to be safe than sorry. Reitzes believes more companies will ultimately turn to Microsoft on the idea that the newer labs are too erratic to plan an entire business implementation around. “We see a credible path for Azure growth to exceed 50% as supply begins to catch up with demand, pricing gets firmer, and OpenAI ramps.” Remember, Microsoft is still a main provider of computing power to OpenAI, even as the relationship between the two companies has evolved since the early days when ChatGPT launched in late 2022 and took the world by storm. That evolution has given Microsoft the freedom to become more model-agnostic. Microsoft has become less focused on the AI model layer and more on the harness layer. We previously discussed the importance of the harness in the context of agentic AI — the model being the brain and the harness as the body that can carry out the actions of the brain and act autonomously without further prompts. “The strategy seems even smarter now given its ‘partners’ are predicting the end of the world — and Microsoft, in essence, can provide Boards with a form of ‘AI insurance,‘” Reitzes said. “Copilot is the front end; Agent 365 provides the registry, security and management layer for agents regardless of the underlying model. … The thought process is that as models become increasingly interchangeable, Microsoft can still capture value by owning the identity, governance, data and billing infrastructure around the agentic workflow. In this framework, the model is increasingly a commodity input while the enterprise harness becomes the strategic control point.” This gets to the heart of the matter. A frontier model alone is not enough to justify the massive levels of capital expenditures from these megacap tech companies. It’s more about what the companies can do with these models that matters to investors. Meta Platforms shares certainly tell that story. The stock has soared more than 20% since the company launched its Muse personal AI agent in early September and then doubled down on a new enterprise endeavor, including Muse for small businesses. It was the “how the model can be used” idea that really moved the needle, even as the strong benchmark results for the Spark model underlying it were well publicized. Bottom line Given that Microsoft is now looking to plant its own major flag at the application layer, but in the enterprise world in which it already dominates, Reitzes’ more optimistic outlook makes perfect sense. With shares now trading only about 3% away from their record-high close of $542 on Oct. 28, 2025, we think this sets the stock up to make a run back to those levels before breaking out further. We have a $550 per share price target on Microsoft. We, however, have a hold equivalent 2 rating because it’s not our style to chase parabolic moves. text:
OpenAI (OPAI.PVT) CEO Sam Altman said that when the company eventually goes public, he plans to continue putting the nonprofit's mission ahead of shareholder interests if the two come into conflict.

In a wide-ranging interview with Vanity Fair that touched on topics including his family, children's use of technology, and AI safety, Altman said that, unlike other companies, OpenAI is governed by its nonprofit arm and that it will continue to dictate how the broader AI lab operates.

"We will remind investors and anyone that thinks about buying our shares that we are going to put the mission first," Altman said. "We believe that that will be compatible with our shareholders doing super well. I genuinely do think that, but if they're ever in tension, the mission is going to come first."

The chief executive added that if OpenAI has to choose between its stock price going up and doing what is right for humanity, it will side with humanity.

"That is part of the reason I think we'll be very successful over time. But if we are wrong about that, and for some reason AI progress is incompatible with making an incredibly valuable company, I really don't think it's the case, I really think these are compatible, we are clearly going to pick doing the right thing for humanity," Altman explained.

OpenAI is widely expected to go public in early 2027. Rival Anthropic (ANTH.PVT) is rumored to be preparing its initial public offering ahead of Thanksgiving.

Conversations around AI safety exploded into the public sphere after OpenAI revealed in late July that its AI models broke free of their restraints during safety testing and hacked into AI database Hugging Face's network.

Since then, Anthropic, Google (GOOG, GOOGL), and Meta (META) have also said that their AI has gotten out during testing.

The hacks and a series of comments from AI researchers raised concerns that AI poses an existential threat to humans. In September, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon posted on X that he was resigning from the company because it and his former employer, OpenAI, are "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."

Anthropic alignment science lead Evan Hubinger responded to Coxon's comments with his own, saying that he believes there is a greater-than-10% chance that the technology could "kill all humans."

text:
Your weekly round-up of the five biggest stories from across the global coffee industry...

Greggs is investing to strengthen its leading market share

Nespresso turns attention to aluminium after pulling the plug on paper capsules

New CEO for Keurig Dr Pepper’s future Global Coffee Co

Retail group takes direct control of key Starbucks markets in East Asia

Luckin Coffee explores Middle East expansion after stake sale

1. Greggs risks rocking the boat in bid to become a 3,500-store brand

Food-to-go and coffee chain Greggs is investing in infrastructure to serve at least 3,500 outlets and to extend its lead as the largest operator in the UK branded coffee shop market.

However, to ensure it can deliver its expansion strategy at scale, Greggs has made a difficult and potentially controversial decision – closing four in-house manufacturing sites and cutting hundreds of jobs.

The move comes amid a purple patch for the popular sausage roll and steak bake maker, with trading across the first nine months of 2026 lifted by new iced beverage, salad and premium hot food ranges.

Will the fiscal reward of consolidating its in-house supply chain outweigh the reputational risk?

2. Nespresso to phase out home compostable paper coffee capsules

Swiss coffee pod giant Nespresso has confirmed that it will phase out its range of home compostable paper capsules, three-and-a-half years after bringing them to market.

The Nestlé-owned B Corp launched the range across 14 European markets, but is now focused on recycling aluminium capsules following concerns over the shelf life of its paper coffee capsules.

Nespresso has over 100,000 dedicated and partner collection points globally for its aluminium capsules, according to its website, including its 800 branded boutique outlets, where it retails its product ranges across 76 markets.

3. Keurig Dr Pepper appoints new CEO for Global Coffee Co spinoff

As part of its $18bn acquisition of JDE Peet’s, Keurig Dr Pepper (KDP) is planning to split into two US-listed companies, Global Coffee Co and Beverage Co, during the first quarter of 2027.

After its initial hire, Rafael Oliveira, U-turned on his decision to lead the future Global Coffee Co, KDP has now appointed a former Kimberly-Clark, Bain and Company and Mondelez International executive to the role.

Tasked with building the company that will “shape the future of coffee”, Russ Torres joins the business at an exciting, but highly pressurised, time.

4. Hong Kong retail group takes control of seven Starbucks markets in East Asia

Hong Kong-based DFI Retail Group has assumed full control of Starbucks operations in seven East Asian markets after joint venture partner Maxim’s Group exited the business.

The deal, which includes 1,100 stores across Hong Kong, Thailand, Singapore, Vietnam, Cambodia, Macau and Laos, is the latest reorganisation of Starbucks’ business in the region.

In April 2026, the US coffee giant sold a $4bn majority stake in its 8,000-store China business to Hong Kong-based investment firm Boyu Capital. Three months later, reports also emerged that Starbucks was exploring a majority stake sale in its highly profitable Japan business.

5. Luckin Coffee eyes Middle East debut after $1bn Mubadala stake sale

Seven years after initially exploring expansion in the Middle East, China’s largest coffee chain is revisiting the idea.

This time, Beijing-based Luckin Coffee is doing so with newly onboarded local expertise, having sold a significant $1bn stake to Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala Investment Company at the start of September 2026.

Luckin has been successful in its international launches to date, rapidly scaling in Malaysia, reaching 100 stores in Singapore and steadily building a notable presence in New York, US.

A Middle East launch would open a new competition front with several scaled Western chains, such as Starbucks, Dunkin’, Tim Hortons and Costa Coffee, while also putting Luckin in direct competition with several of the Middle East’s fastest-growing branded coffee chains.

text:
Axa is simultaneously pruning geopolitical exposure, planting a flag in the US wholesale insurance market and shielding its share count from dilution — a three-track maneuver that says as much about what the French insurer wants to avoid as what it wants to own.

At the center of the retreat sits the International Criminal Court in The Hague. Axa and the tribunal mutually agreed to terminate their health insurance contract, with the court signaling it will seek a new provider. The insurer attributed the decision to risks stemming from the extraterritorial reach of US sanctions, according to Reuters. It is a quiet exit, but a telling one: Axa is treating regulatory spillover as a live underwriting hazard rather than an abstract legal footnote.

Building Where the Margins Are

While one door closes, another is being fitted with a new sign. Axa's large-corporate arm, AXA XL, has stood up the AXA XL Excess & Surplus Lines Insurance Company, a US carrier built to serve wholesale brokers. The liability book is scheduled to begin writing business in early 2027, with existing liability policies migrating at mid-year. Property coverage will follow later in 2027, completing a staged rollout that keeps capital deployment tethered to underwriting discipline rather than launch-day ambition.

Leadership for the push is being assembled in parallel. AXA XL named Dr. Thomas Götting as Chief Client & Distribution Officer for APAC & Europe, handing him the client and distribution strategy across Europe, Asia and Australia. In the UK and Lloyd's market, Debbie Durkan stepped into the role of Head of Private Equity and Business Development — a pair of appointments that signal the specialty unit is staffing for relationships, not just capacity.

Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Axa?

Trimming the European Back Office

Efficiency work is proceeding on the other side of the Atlantic. Following the merger of its Commercial and Retail divisions, AXA Insurance UK has placed 60 positions at risk of redundancy, spread across risk, compliance and governance functions, according to media reports. The cuts are administrative rather than underwriting-related, consistent with a group-wide effort to keep the expense base from expanding alongside its specialty ambitions.

A Buyback With a Specific Job

Capital returns are being deployed with a narrow mandate. Axa has struck an agreement to repurchase up to EUR 470.8 million of its own shares, which will subsequently be cancelled. The purpose is not a broad shareholder payout but a targeted offset: neutralizing the dilutive effect of the Shareplan 2026 employee participation program. The buybacks are slated for completion no later than October 29, 2026.

The insurer's scale underpins the maneuver. Axa carries a market capitalization of EUR 87.96 billion, keeping it firmly among Europe's largest insurance groups.

Axa at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now.

Where the Stock Stands

The equity traded at EUR 42.24 on the day, a gain of 0.7%. That level sits comfortably above the 200-day moving average of EUR 41.51, a technical marker that suggests the shares have held their footing through a period of structural change.

Taken together, the moving pieces sketch a company that is deliberately trading breadth for control — exiting a mandate where sanctions risk outweighed the premium, funding a US specialty buildout with staged timelines, and using buybacks to keep per-share economics intact while employees take up stock. Growth is on the agenda, but only where the risk map has been redrawn first.

Zurich Insurance Group has completed its acquisition of UK-based insurer Beazley, with the combined business holding gross written premiums of around $15bn.

Kristof Terryn has been named CEO of Beazley and Zurich Global Specialty, subject to regulatory approval.

Current CEO Adrian Cox is leaving Beazley as the company starts its next phase.

Helen Pickford, CFO of Zurich UK, will become CFO of Beazley and Zurich Global Specialty.

Barbara Plucnar Jensen, Beazley Group CFO, will support the integration as a senior adviser until March 2027.

Sally Henderson and Ed Bridge will become chief people and sustainability officer and general counsel, respectively, at Beazley and Zurich Global Specialty.

title: OpenAI safety employee David Robinson resigns, warns on AI culture - Quartz
description:
Robinson, who said he is among the longest-tenured employees at OpenAI with three and a half years at the company, wrote in The Atlantic that OpenAI's "culture is broken."
"As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed," Robinson wrote.
OpenAI's safety incidents have included agents accessing government websites in the U.S. and Australia during training runs and a July breach of the Hugging Face platform.
The company terminated three safety researchers last week for allegedly sharing confidential information with a third-party AI safety organization.
OpenAI has also opened its safety evaluations to outside organizations throughout the training and deployment process, extending access that had been limited to pre-launch checks.
text:
David Robinson, who led transparency work on OpenAI's safety team, resigned from the company last week and published an essay warning that top AI firms are not doing enough to mitigate the risks posed by the technology, according to TechCrunch.

Robinson, who said he is among the longest-tenured employees at OpenAI with three and a half years at the company, wrote in The Atlantic that OpenAI's "culture is broken." He argued that the company's reliance on what it terms "iterative deployment" — essentially learning by doing — inherently produces mistakes, and that the potential damage from those mistakes is escalating as the underlying technology grows more powerful, according to TechCrunch.

"As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed," Robinson wrote.

Robinson called on leading AI companies to adopt the operational disciplines of industries like nuclear energy and commercial aviation, where overlapping safeguards and deliberate, time-intensive planning keep human mistakes from spiraling into catastrophe. He added that throughout his tenure at OpenAI, he never worked alongside anyone who had built expertise in those high-stakes fields — whether in aviation safety, nuclear operations, or financial system oversight, according to TechCrunch.

Robinson cited concrete episodes to make his case that OpenAI's current operating culture is ill-equipped for building ever-more-capable AI systems — including an intrusion into the Hugging Face platform carried out by OpenAI agents and a string of reported instances in which agents went rogue during testing, according to TechCrunch.

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the outlet that the company is tightening security across its research and testing environments, working to ensure models complete tasks responsibly, broadening its engagement with third-party evaluators, and enhancing real-time monitoring to identify concerning model behavior at an earlier stage of training. The company is also ensuring its models do not become more capable than it can safely manage, Pusateri said.

Robinson's departure comes amid a wave of safety-related warnings from researchers across the industry. OpenAI's safety incidents have included agents accessing government websites in the U.S. and Australia during training runs and a July breach of the Hugging Face platform. The company terminated three safety researchers last week for allegedly sharing confidential information with a third-party AI safety organization. OpenAI has also opened its safety evaluations to outside organizations throughout the training and deployment process, extending access that had been limited to pre-launch checks.

Robinson acknowledged that remaining at the company to drive reform from the inside was something he weighed, but concluded it was not realistic given the environment. "My colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them," he wrote.

name: OpenAI
title: OpenAI's safety firings raise awkward questions - Fortune
description:
That same week, OpenAI also fired three researchers for allegedly sharing confidential company information with a third-party AI-safety organization.
OpenAI has reportedly fired three safety researchers for sharing information with an outside AI safety group.
Here, it seems like the disclosures were to external AI safety organizations.
The FTC also launched an investigation into AI safety practices at Anthropic and OpenAI.
The firings also weren’t the only safety departure at OpenAI last week.
text:
That same week, OpenAI also fired three researchers for allegedly sharing confidential company information with a third-party AI-safety organization. They were Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak, and Mikita Balesni; according to the Wall Street Journal.

OpenAI told the WSJ they had been fired for “violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information.” The company did not respond to our request for comment.

It’s not known yet exactly what information was shared or who they shared it with, though Bloomberg reported that at least some of the information at the center of the investigation related to the architecture of OpenAI’s infrastructure. OpenAI also hasn’t named the outside organization, and the three researchers haven’t commented publicly.

Still, the terminations have the internet locked in a fierce debate—and have caught the attention of lawmakers.

Congressman Greg Casar wrote: “Outrageous. OpenAI has reportedly fired three safety researchers for sharing information with an outside AI safety group. This looks like they’re firing whistleblowers. What are they hiding? I’ll be sending OpenAI a demand for transparency.”

The terminations come at a time when OpenAI and rival AI labs are under increasing pressure to be more transparent about safety incidents. OpenAI, in particular, has been heavily criticized by the industry for delays in disclosing incidents, particularly one in which its agents hijacked a German wiki site, something the company reportedly knew about for months but failed to disclose until it was revealed by independent researchers.

Should OpenAI have been quicker to disclose some of these hacks? Absolutely, and the company has conceded it needs clearer standards for doing so. But it isn’t clear that what the fired employees allegedly shared had anything to do with those incidents. And even if it did, whether that makes them whistleblowers is complicated.

Here’s what Charlie Bullock, a senior policy director for LawAI’s U.S. Law and Policy team, had to say:

I don’t have a firm opinion on the OpenAI firings yet, because I don’t know what information the employees shared or whom they shared it with.

Generally, though, existing law protects California whistleblowers from being fired for blowing the whistle only when they disclose information to the government or law enforcement, or internally within their company—not when they disclose information to private third parties or the press.

Here, it seems like the disclosures were to external AI safety organizations. That kind of disclosure is not protected by any law that I’m aware of, and IMO it probably shouldn’t be.

Of course, none of that necessarily means that it was right or acceptable for OpenAI to fire these employees. But I’ll withhold judgment on that until we know more about what happened.

Based on what’s known so far, the researchers likely wouldn’t qualify for legal whistleblower protection, as Bullock says. But the firings still put OpenAI in an awkward spot. The company is drawing a line between sanctioned and unsanctioned sharing with outside safety groups at the same time the industry is, slowly, inviting those groups in.

Last month, Anthropic said it would let outside evaluators like METR verify its safety practices and assess its models. OpenAI opened its own doors to METR and Redwood Research for six days after its agents hacked Hugging Face. OpenAI was also criticized at the time for the lack of time and access it granted METR to investigate the hack, and Korbak, one of the fired researchers, says he was the company’s technical contact for that investigation.

Regulators are also beginning to demand more transparency and responsibility from the labs. In September, for example, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said OpenAI’s management needed to take responsibility for the recent agent hacks. Last week, California Attorney General Rob Bonta issued an investigative subpoena to OpenAI as part of a broader inquiry into cybersecurity incidents and risks related to its AI models. The FTC also launched an investigation into AI safety practices at Anthropic and OpenAI.

And, also last week, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, xAI, and Nvidia signed a voluntary White House pact that commits them to partnering with independent external auditors.

The firings also weren’t the only safety departure at OpenAI last week. David Robinson, who led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches, resigned and published an essay in The Atlantic arguing the company’s culture is broken. Robinson argued that AI companies can’t be relied on to police themselves, and that real pressure to prioritize safety has to come from outside.

All of this makes the recent terminations tricky for OpenAI and shows that safety disclosures are still very much at the whims of the labs. Right now, in part because of a lack of government intervention, the companies are the only ones deciding what the public knows about these hacks.

title: As OpenAI and Anthropic battle over data privacy, more companies turn to open models
description:
OpenAI and Anthropic have stated they do not train their models on enterprise data.
Still, many data security experts say the AI companies may have subtler ways to glean insights about how their customers’ operate that can be used to improve future AI models, without having to train directly on the data the models’ are processing.
Given these concerns, companies are looking to diversify their AI usage, and reduce their dependency on the leading AI companies.
Bedrock is an entrypoint for companies to access multiple AI models, without the providers seeing their data.
“It’s a more established company people have been using for decades.” Open models require more oversight—and obtaining GPUs Many companies are adopting a “hybrid model,” Gregory said, meaning they are using some combination of closed models and open source models.
text:
The biggest controversy came in June, when Anthropic began mandating a 30-day retention policy for all chats with its most powerful AI models, Fable and Mythos. Many companies had an “almost allergic reaction” to this, says a source who advises clients on becoming AI-native, speaking under the condition of anonymity because his company works closely with Anthropic. “The industry at large totally rejected it, and was pretty angry about it.”

A month later, both Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and Palantir CEO Alex Karp warned companies against relying on AI models from frontier AI companies, saying that they risked having the IP siphoned off. “You essentially pay for intelligence twice, once with money, and again with something even more valuable: the proprietary knowledge you must reveal to make that intelligence useful,” Nadella said. OpenAI and Anthropic have stated they do not train their models on enterprise data.

Still, many data security experts say the AI companies may have subtler ways to glean insights about how their customers’ operate that can be used to improve future AI models, without having to train directly on the data the models’ are processing. “From a business standpoint, the risk of any of that data being trained on an AI model is unacceptable,” Rob Gregory, Vice President and Chief Information Security Officer at Optiv, a B2B cybersecurity advisory company, tells Fortune. “We’re at a very interesting crossroad.”

The latest string of “rogue AI” incidents have heightened fears that the latest models will either scrape data, or publish it for the world to see, without the business’ permission.

Given these concerns, companies are looking to diversify their AI usage, and reduce their dependency on the leading AI companies. The term du jour for this is “sovereign AI,” referring to a company’s ability to control its own “AI stack”—everything from owning the chips on which AI workloads run, to setting up proprietary cloud infrastructure, to using open source models that a company can download and run in their own cloud environments.

Sovereign AI is a term that has historically been associated with governments, but this year its usage has bled into the corporate world.

“Data sovereignty is something we’re talking a lot about,” said Brooke Hopkins, founder of voice AI company Coval. Dutta also said sovereign AI has “been a large topic of conversation for us over the past few months.”

The problem is that running open source AI models requires more technical expertise and, in some cases, may also mean that companies are not getting the cutting-edge capabilities, in areas such as coding or financial analysis, that some of the products from the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google offer. “You’re trading control for responsibility, right?” Gregory said. “Because there is a significant amount of responsibility when you bring that internally.”

OpenAI and Anthropic are still earning trust

Anthropic and OpenAI are competing directly to win over business customers, and keep the ones they have from either switching companies or seeking open source alternatives.

OpenAI saw an opening to win customers after Anthropic’s data retention announcement, and in an August 19 blog post reiterated that it offers full ZDR for enterprise customers, while also previewing a new feature called Private Safety Processing (PSP). PSP adds a data storage element to ZDR, while also offering a system in which customers can store data in their own cloud, rather than on OpenAI’s servers.

Anthropic responded on Sept. 1 with a new, similar version of ZDR that also offers businesses a way to store their data on their own cloud accounts—not Anthropic’s. But has the damage already been done? After the company announced its 30-day retention policy, businesses like Booz Allen decided to restrict their teams’ use of its Fable model, The Information reported.

Another common route for businesses to use leading models from these companies is through Amazon Bedrock. Bedrock is an entrypoint for companies to access multiple AI models, without the providers seeing their data. It’s one of the fastest growing AWS products of all time, with customer spend growing 170% in Q1, and nearly 80% adoption by the Fortune 100.

“Amazon is like, ‘You don’t have to trust the frontier labs,’” said Randall Hunt, chief technology officer at Caylent, an AWS advisory company. “It’s a more established company people have been using for decades.”

Open models require more oversight—and obtaining GPUs

Many companies are adopting a “hybrid model,” Gregory said, meaning they are using some combination of closed models and open source models.

“Sovereign AI basically enables you to say, ‘Okay, I will continue to partner with OpenAI and Anthropic for some things, but maybe here’s another set of use cases that I want to use open source models for on prem,” Dutta added.

But this requires companies themselves to secure the models and implement them responsibly. Glen Wise, CEO and co-founder of Cinder, which makes software that helps detect and remediate model abuse, has seen a spike in inbound customer requests since Anthropic announced Fable would not have ZDR. “We’ve already been working with the main model creators, but in the past few weeks we have started getting requests from regular companies that are trying to figure out how to deploy open models,” Wise said.

Businesses with particularly sensitive data, such as health records, are not shying away from these added responsibilities, and some are even taking it a step further by running open models on their own GPUs, essentially becoming miniature data center owners. Payroll company Paycom told Fortune it has taken this approach because of the sensitive customer data and financial information it handles.

This is still relatively uncommon, but some people think it will prove to be the smartest long-term strategy.

“There’s a big shift going on, whereas in the past 25 years, [businesses would] pick your hyper-scalers, and then just let them take care of all things compute,” said Dan Wright, the founder and CEO of Armada, which makes portable data centers and will provide the infrastructure for Palantir and Nvidia’s forthcoming joint offering to help other businesses adopt fully sovereign AI. Crusoe,another company that has pivoted from building massive data centers to focusing on tiny ones. It was recently valued at $31 billion in a venture capital round earlier this month, according to the Wall Street Journal. “This is very much the direction the market is going,” Wright said.

But not every company is as anxious about data and IP leaking to the AI companies. “While I need to be paranoid about my IP, I trust the big AI companies are going to do the right thing because we’re both on the line to make sure it’s secure,” said Dan Cane, co-CEO of ModMed.

name: Microsoft
title: Satya Nadella reinvented Microsoft once. Can he do it again in the AI era? - CNBC
description:
Sven Hoppe | Picture Alliance | Getty Images On a sunny day in Seattle in late September, about 50 executives representing large Microsoft customers had a rare opportunity.
For longtime Microsoft investors, Nadella has a solid track record when it comes to navigating industry shifts.
"GitHub Copilot went out and learned lessons," said Kyle Daigle, the unit's operating chief, in an interview.
At the September Copilot event, Nadella stood before a slide declaring that Copilot could connect to "every model," with the Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX and Microsoft AI logos.
While Nadella earned investor trust in reviving Microsoft once, he can't afford to let the company become an also-ran in AI.
text:
Sven Hoppe | Picture Alliance | Getty Images

On a sunny day in Seattle in late September, about 50 executives representing large Microsoft customers had a rare opportunity. They could ask anything of CEO Satya Nadella.

One attendee wanted to know what Microsoft could do to help companies adapt to the artificial intelligence age. Nadella responded by emphasizing the importance of "diffusion inside the enterprise," meaning AI tools need to be widely deployed.

"Like all things, change is always bottom up, top down, and middle up," said Nadella, sporting a tight black crewneck and dark gray slacks, as he strode across the stage at the downtown Paccar Pavilion.

For the 59-year-old Nadella, who's spent over half his life at Microsoft, the gathering landed at a pivotal moment, as the software giant tries to magnify its role in the AI boom. Of late, Nadella has been inserting himself more into the AI discourse, posting on X last month about the need for "deliberate pacing" in model development, and days later addressing safety fears at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles.

Despite its almost $4 trillion market cap, Microsoft has yet to break out as an AI leader. Nvidia dominates in AI chips, Anthropic and OpenAI boast the foremost models, Meta just released the first mass-market personal agent, and Google's Gemini-powered services are popular with businesses and consumers.

Microsoft was aggressively early to AI through an investment in OpenAI, but that alliance has frayed. While the software giant has a big business in renting out chips for AI developers through its Azure cloud, its Copilot technology isn't pervasive in the workplace, and its proprietary AI models remain niche.

The company is hosting a Windows and Surface event in San Francisco on Wednesday, describing it in an invitation as "a conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC."

Wall Street is lukewarm on the story. Even factoring in a sharp third-quarter rally, the stock is trailing its megacap peers and the broader Nasdaq this year, up just 7% as of Friday's close. Microsoft hasn't beaten the S&P 500 in a calendar year since 2023.

Stock Chart IconStock chart icon

Tiffany Wade, co-portfolio manager at Microsoft shareholder Columbia Threadneedle, said there are a lot of unknowns about Copilot, which is the centerpiece of Nadella's AI strategy.

"I think there needs to be a little bit more maturity of the product before we figure out actually what the best solution or what pricing is," Wade said in an interview.

For longtime Microsoft investors, Nadella has a solid track record when it comes to navigating industry shifts. He was named CEO in 2014, succeeding Steve Ballmer, who had presided over a roughly 33% drop in the stock price during his 14-year tenure, as Microsoft slipped into the beleaguered category of legacy software.

Nadella proceeded to turn Microsoft into a cloud powerhouse. He tossed aside perpetual Office software licenses and pushed the company into subscription-based software-as-a-service offerings alongside Azure infrastructure. And he permitted customers to integrate products from bitter rivals like Oracle and Salesforce , rather than insisting on a pure Microsoft stack.

Trained as an electrical engineer and computer scientist, Nadella became a savvy dealmaker, expanding Microsoft through acquisitions of "Minecraft"-maker Mojang, business social network LinkedIn and code-sharing service GitHub.

In recent months, Nadella has acknowledged to investors that he's got to change the business model yet again, this time to reflect the AI-fueled move toward consumption-based pricing. That means becoming a vendor of large volumes of tokens, which measure computing usage and represent the currency of the AI economy.

Success would mean "further expanding our TAM," Nadella said on Microsoft's July earnings call, adopting the acronym for total addressable market.

Much of the growth story Nadella preaches involves the production of software. Develop more code and do it faster, boosted by the latest and greatest AI tools.

"We went from the code assist to the agentic coding to software factory all within one year," Nadella said at the customer gathering late last month.

Now he wants to see Microsoft clients open their own software factories, spending more along the way to help churn out code. He's also hoping to empower non-technical knowledge workers. Some of Nadella's lieutenants at the event unveiled a Copilot "super app" that can perform increasingly complex tasks, generate simple applications and function as a virtual teammate.

Nadella had a preview of what was coming.

Microsoft first invested in OpenAI in 2019, when the company was still a fledgling lab. In 2021, a year before ChatGPT launched, Microsoft and OpenAI collaborated to release GitHub Copilot, a tool that could write parts of applications and websites based on vast swaths of public source code.

They'd created an early sensation. But as the generative AI market took off, developers moved to products from AI-native startups like Cursor, now owned by SpaceX , and Anthropic, which rolled out Claude Code.

'Learned lessons'

Microsoft's sluggishness in keeping up with the rapid changes cost GitHub market share.

Earlier this year, Microsoft adjusted the pricing for the coding tool to align more with computing demand. Some customers initially balked, but by July the company said it had racked up 50 million users, up from 26 million last October, meaning that one in five on GitHub were on board.

Nadella said on the July earnings call that GitHub Copilot sales growth accelerated 60% from the previous quarter, with "significant consumption revenue after the new model went into effect."

"GitHub Copilot went out and learned lessons," said Kyle Daigle, the unit's operating chief, in an interview.

Daigle said GitHub employees shared their lessons with other teams at Microsoft that are eyeing consumption-based pricing schemes.

Hayete Gallot, Microsoft's executive vice president for security products, said the company will charge clients according to how intensely they use the technology.

"I always say to my team, when customers consume, it means we add value. And for me, the truth starts with customers," Gallot said. "If they don't consume, it means we're not giving value."

Currently, Microsoft's enterprise portfolio is reliant on subscriptions. For its core Microsoft 365 productivity suite, which includes Word, Excel and Teams, customers sign up for years at a time, and Copilot costs an extra $30 per person each month. Microsoft has 30 million Copilot seats. The commercial Office 365 base exceeds 450 million.

Stephen Brashear | Getty Images News | Getty Images

One area of uncertainty in Microsoft's AI roadmap revolves around Mustafa Suleyman.

Suleyman previously co-founded AI lab DeepMind, which Google bought in 2014. Nadella hired him in 2024 to lead AI initiatives as Microsoft's relationship with OpenAI was cooling.

Last year, Microsoft lost its status as OpenAI's exclusive cloud provider, and this year its license on OpenAI intellectual property became non-exclusive. That left the software company with a massive investment in the AI lab but less preferential treatment. Microsoft said in April that it continues to serve as OpenAI's "primary cloud partner."

Suleyman's group has rolled out models for coding, image generation and reasoning. This week he boasted on X that a new speech-to-text model was "the most accurate real time transcription model in the world... #1 !!!" But for raw digital intellect, the team has yet to rival Anthropic or OpenAI, according to independent leaderboards.

Microsoft executives say there are benefits to having model and application development under the same roof. The group building Teams and other Office productivity apps has seen higher performance from Suleyman's transcription models at a lower price, and engineers get clear feedback as they build out products, said Executive Vice President Charles Lamanna.

"The collaboration is much tighter with Mustafa," he said.

Suleyman maintains a high profile at Microsoft, but his responsibilities have shifted. In March, Microsoft announced that it was bringing together the engineering groups for its commercial and consumer Copilot assistants, as adoption had been sluggish. Jacob Andreou was promoted to executive vice president for Copilot experience, and Suleyman was charged with focusing on model development.

Nadella, meanwhile, has been downplaying the importance of world-beating models in isolation.

"In my view, our priority has to be building a frontier ecosystem, not just a frontier model, so value flows broadly across every company, every industry, and every country," he wrote in a post on his SN Scratchpad website in June.

At the September Copilot event, Nadella stood before a slide declaring that Copilot could connect to "every model," with the Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX and Microsoft AI logos.

Fixing the economics

Increasingly, Microsoft is finding the model leaders encroaching on its turf, as they release products for cybersecurity, customer service and other functions.

In January, as Anthropic's Claude Code was building momentum, Microsoft executives were impressed with its ability to tap a bevy of tools to get things done, said Jared Spataro, Microsoft's marketing chief for AI at work. Microsoft was losing deals to Anthropic, promoting a close study of a rising competitor, said a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named due to confidentiality.

A Microsoft spokesperson declined to comment.

Spataro said the company sensed a need to change the mechanics.

"It became very clear to us at that moment. Like, oh wow, the economics are not going to be such that we're going to be able to offer now the best outcome within a fixed price per user per month," Spataro said. "We realized that we needed to start to think about the business model."

The company got cracking on a more comprehensive approach to consumption-based pricing that it calls usage-based billing, or UBB. The first UBB product was Copilot Cowork, which accepts large productivity assignments and shows its progress, Spataro said.

Nadella said on the July earnings call that "earlier this month, we added usage-based billing to Cowork with thousands of customers already paying for and actively using it."

Courtesy: Microsoft

Derrick Wood, an analyst at Cowen, said it was a strong signal.

"It may have the effect of what we saw when Claude Code, for example, shifted to consumption pricing, and you saw token bills go significantly higher," said Wood, who recommends buying Microsoft shares. "There's definitely the possibility for that to happen with Cowork."

Nadella is a user. On a podcast recorded after the September event, he said he can ask Cowork to prepare a supply chain optimization spreadsheet showing multiple scenarios.

"It'll create a fantastic artifact," he said.

David Berry, a vice president at advisory group Directions on Microsoft, said budget-conscious IT executives aren't all ready to take the Cowork plunge.

"There's a very real concern that you just kind of turn it on and people are going to start draining the bank," Berry said. "There's no way to determine if people are actually getting any benefit from it."

With the ChatGPT era nearing its four-year anniversary, Microsoft is still looking for a smash hit, whether at the model or application layer. While Nadella earned investor trust in reviving Microsoft once, he can't afford to let the company become an also-ran in AI.

Berry said he still sees Nadella as the right person to command the ship.

"He seems to be able to handle the situations or identify the situations and come up with a plan to change and evolve the business," he said. "The challenge is we're facing a lot more of the unknowns in a sense with AI, so it's a lot of different market dynamics going on, but he seems to have a plan, and he's working the plan."

In Seattle, Nadella ended his response to the transformation question by saying that those at the top of organizations play a key role.

"Leaders who are hands-on are able to change," he said. "Otherwise, they're all from press event to press event, right?"

He added, "It's kind of like you've got to be in it."

title: Carbon Capture Is Coming For Cement's CO2 Emissions
description:
Carbon capture isn’t just an option for cement – it’s the only way to tackle the industry’s fundamental chemistry problem.
From Brevik to the Next Generation of Cement CCS Brevik matters because it proved cement CCS can survive contact with commercial reality.
That hard floor is why carbon capture sits at the center of long-term decarbonization planning.
